In a fourth MMORPG... well that game is toxic-as-fuck, but I think that's because it's a free to play game modelled to be exactly like the first one. I do however still disagree with the direction its latest expansion is going. Some of my biggest criticisms include: 1. Starting players with 12 workers instead of 6 is going to kill a lot of low-income cheese builds, which actually made the game interesting. These days, fast expand builds are going to be mandatory because of how kickstarted the economy already is. It's quite sad, really because a popular multiplayer game proves that taking gameplay choices away from players equals a shittier game. 2. Reducing the amount of minerals per base by 25% (by halving the minerals on half of the nodes) is a suboptimal solution at fixing the strategy game's flawed mining system. Adjusting minerals does not change this but rather punishes defensive play and falling behind on bases far more severely than earlier versions did. This time, losing expansions will become game-ending and games will end much, much faster. 3. Apart from the Lurker (which is a very welcome addition to the Zerg arsenal), there aren't any units or balance changes that improve the defensive capabilities of any particular race. Siege Tanks for instance are even shittier and less viable in the new expansion than they were in earlier versions because now they're **HUGELY** vulnerable to Ravagers and Disruptors. If the developers want more players to take expansions in the new expansion, then they need to give each race the tools to defend said bases. And that means buffing Siege Tanks and Colossi to fill these niches. 4. Terran in particular got shafted. The Cyclone is suboptimal, too expensive, too slow to build, and too late in the tech tree to be viable in any Mech build. Meanwhile the Liberator is a shit jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none unit that does things which other ground and air units can do 10 times better.

A similar company pretty much did the same thing with a legacy version of their game when they shut down a popular private server. They took on-board the feedback of how many people hated the modern version and its various changes, saw that the legacy version was gaining a lot of hype, and gave their fanbase what they wanted. Fun fact, the legacy version is now the *most popular* version of the game, regularly managing more active players at once than the modern version, and that is only set to grow even further when the legacy dev team plan a phased-release of a brand new content exclusive to the legacy version which will increase the size of the game world immensely at the beginning of 2016. That's right, the legacy version is so popular that the company is releasing *new* content for that version of the game. While I won't go so far as to say the major developer needs to release new legacy content, a launch of legacy servers running on legacy versions of the game client is what the developer needs to be doing with their main game. If the developer made an old-school client available and allowed subscribers to download the older clients and experience the game as it was originally intended, I would resub in a heartbeat. Hell, even if they did a similar thing and hired a few extra devs to produce new content for the legacy game such as the (originally intended) raid and slew of cut zones and islands in that era, then I can see Legacy realms eclipsing the current release realms with absolute ease. It's quite sad that you can only experience the previous game world, and the original class abilities, talents and itemisation which fuelled the game these days by playing on a private server. Meanwhile on retail, any content outside of specific dungeon modes remains abandoned, and cannot be experienced at its originally intended difficulty level even if you could 'level down' your character like in other games thanks to years and years of immense power creep through really horribly designed game updates. The developer say it's too hard, or 'the technology simply isn't there', but there are people who have reverse-engineered the older clients and managed to run a slew of private servers which have both emulated and built upon a similar experience. I cannot think of a smarter analogy than this, but imagine if you purchased the game's Battle Chest only to then find out that you are unable to access anything in the campaign other than the latest expansion, because to the devs, the latest expansion is the current content and you should not care about anything except the latest content. Ahhh, a typical "Just make more money" argument. For a lot of people, this simply isn't an option. Let's say you work in retail or customer service and earn the minimum wage, which a lot of people do. The average full time contract is for a standard number of hours per week, and the national minimum wage is a specific hourly rate (for a worker over a certain age, whereas it gets even lower for anyone below that age.) Hence, a worker in that bracket can earn a modest weekly amount, a yearly amount, or an monthly amount in pre-tax pay. Now let's subtract taxation and national insurance contributions from this figure. [Rather than bore you with lots of mathematical calculations, I found a website capable of calculating the income](https://www.incometaxcalculator.org.uk/?ingr=14040&time=1&yr=2017&age=0#). This gives us a net annual wage (rounded to nearest penny) of a specific amount per year, a monthly amount, a weekly amount, or an hourly amount. Since employees are usually paid at the end of the month, we're now concerned with the net monthly figure. [Let's subtract the average monthly energy bill on a small house/flat from that figure](https://www.ukpower.co.uk/home_energy/average-energy-bill), which is a certain amount per month, [then subtract food and internet from that monthly bill, on the assumption that the worker is living the austere lifestyle of a student.](http://www.ed.ac.uk/studying/international/finance/cost-of-living) This means that we now have an income per month after taxation and basic necessities (gas/electricity, groceries/food, internet connection, which is almost mandatory in today's society, and is required to play World of Warcraft, so screw it, we're factoring this in as well.) Since we're now concerned with the disposable income of a minimum wage worker, let's compare the monthly income to [average rent prices in a major metropolitan area, according to statistics quoted by local media:](http://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/property/11984097/London-rents-now-a-record-108pc-higher-than-rest-of-UK.html) * The major city - There is no way that anybody on a salary that low can live there with its average rent costs. The city is just *that* heavily price gouged due to overpopulation, gentrification, and heavy demand for properties. Even most residents can barely afford to live there on their increased average salaries compared to the rest of the country. * The surrounding region - Perhaps if you're lucky enough to find a cheap property far away from the city to rent, you could maybe live a very austere life there. Otherwise, good luck, because the region is populated pretty highly with workers who commute into the city on a regular basis. * Another region - At a certain monthly cost, the average property is pretty unaffordable and will leave you living an incredibly austere lifestyle. * Another region - At a certain monthly cost, we finally have a point where we can calculate the percentage of disposable income that a WoW realm transfer priced at a specific amount would be: a calculation resulting in a high percentage of your disposable income. * Another region - At a lower monthly cost, the percentage of disposable income that a WoW realm transfer would cost would be: a calculation resulting in a lower percentage. With the rest of monthly rent prices being very close to the previous figure, and being at most a certain amount lower, let's not calculate the rest. Rent alone costs a huge amount of money for a resident, and on top of having to pay out of our ass for other necessities, the price of a WoW realm transfer isn't justified just to be able to play a dying game with many servers resembling ghost towns.

It is almost undisputably the worst console to be released in the last fifteen years. Other notoriously shit consoles from the last fifteen years like the N-Gage and the Gizmondo had far more redeeming qualities than Nintendo's did. _____________________________ **The first fatal flaw was its shitty storage.** Bundling a console in 2012 with only 8 GB (or 32 GB with the Deluxe model) of internal storage was a stupid idea. For comparison, the original Xbox which released back in 2002 has the same amount of internal storage space as the Basic model of the Wii U. For the Xbox, this was amazing because back in 2002 when gamers didn't have to worry about buying games digitally, or downloading massive launch day patches, 8GB of space was far more than plenty to hold the save game data of any hardcore gamer's library, unlike the expensive proprietary memory cards Nintendo and Sony forced down their players' throats which generally had just a few MBs of storage (the standard GC card had 4MB, the PS2 card had 8MB, and the larger capacity GC card which glitched out with certain games like Phantasy Star Online had 16MB in comparison.) Nowadays, you have digital game downloads which would fail to even fit on a Basic Wii U, and which would barely fit on a Deluxe model. This wouldn't even be so bad if Nintendo supported decent methods of external storage. Yes, there was SD card support, but that was exclusive to the Wii compatibility mode and could never be used to store Wii U downloadable content or games. Instead, gamers had to rely on external hard drives, and often ones with their own external power supply to ensure the games you downloaded didn't glitch out or crash from a lack of power. As the owner of an external drive without its own external power plug, I've been unable to play certain games which support external storage really badly like the Wii U digital release of Metroid Prime Trilogy, because the game just fucking glitches out on the tutorial every time. And let's say you *did* use such an external HDD which Nintendo officially recommends; you've now got three power plugs: one for the console, one for charging the bulky gamepad and one for powering the external drive. [While the power adaptors are far from bulky, this is very similar to why the AVGN slagged off the 32X and Sega CD addons](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VvR_3OTxs8A) _____________________________ **The second fatal flaw is the Gamepad.** It's bulky, it's gimmicky, it doesn't feel natural unlike the DS and 3DS usage of dual screens, and when games force gyroscopic controls and Gamepad aiming upon you, it becomes cancer. At least with the DS and 3DS, you only have to direct your vision a little bit higher up to see the top screen, and both screens sync together in a lot of games almost flawlessly. With the Wii U Gamepad, you have to look straight down at the Gamepad whenever you want to look at the menu or use an item that requires you to use the touchscreen, or face the Gamepad right in front of you like an oversized steering wheel just to see both the TV and Gamepad screens in your vision simultaneously. The gyroscopic controls are also horseshit in comparison to the 3DS, partially due to the fact that you're using a bulky gamepad instead of a slim, sleek handheld console to aim, but also partially due to the fact that it was awfully calibrated in comparison to the 3DS. How could Nintendo get a concept that worked perfectly in Ocarina of Time 3D and Majora's Mask 3D to the point where gyroscopic aiming actually outperformed analogue aiming with the circle pad, and fuck it up royally with Star Fox Zero and Splatoon which are good games hampered by their horrible controls... ______________________________ **And finally, leading to the final fatal flaw, which the gimmicky Gamepad was largely responsible for.... the price tag and technical specificications.** For your $350 USD, you could get a PS3 with a slightly inferior GPU and a superior CPU for *less than half the price*. Hence, what gamers got with the Wii U was a gimmicky, low spec console with its price hammered up by a mandatory freakishly-sized touchscreen tablet Gamepad controller that the Wii U couldn't operate without. Yes, many official Nintendo titles had official 1080p and 60FPS support, but even Nintendo hit a ceiling, especially with the HD remake of Wind Waker which was capped at 30FPS. I'm personally fine with the ability to pay for competitive advantages, so long as the business model is reasonable and doesn't require you to sink thousands of dollars a month in order to compete, just like with a popular mobile strategy game. The developers have to make their money from somewhere, and while Free-to-Play models certainly spark an increase in the number of consumers playing your game, it's the fact that a vast majority of them will play without paying a dime that makes F2P models flawed. Then there's the question of what defines P2W in a video game. Is it the competitive advantage gained from faster progression (i.e. a major MMORPG, a popular MOBA, a tank simulator), or is it the competitive advantage gained from premium items which you can only reasonably obtain with real world money (i.e. a hero shooter, a card game if you don't already have a competitive deck, a fantasy RPG, a first-person shooter, also a tank simulator with its premium tanks and 'Free XP' which can only be unlocked with gold purchased via real world cash.) Then there's also the question of whether faster progression competitively affects the game. In a game like a popular mobile strategy game, production boosts and shields can only be purchased with premium gems and are generally required to compete at a high level, unlike with a popular MOBA where one hero purchase with premium currency or Influence Points (non premium currency which you grind) is permanent.

The grass textures and skybox in particular look dated in retrospect. * There are very limited options for increasing the rendering distance of foliage (without mods), meaning that you'll still have instances where grass straight up disappears and becomes a flat texture from a few dozen yards away. * HDR lighting and anti-aliasing are mutually exclusive. Why? * No Borderless or Windowed (Fullscreen) option is quite bad for a game from that era. This was something a popular MMORPG had during its early days and that game came out earlier. Instead, we only have the choice of Fullscreen or Windowed. Hell, Borderless wasn't even patched in to the game.  * Why is the 'Ultra High' quality preset on the Options menu set to a low resolution? If you're looking at a lake or river from a distance, the reflection will look incredibly pixellated, even on maximum settings. * Having every town, city and DLC quest location unlocked as a fast travel point from the get-go completely ruins the exploration aspect of the game, especially if you're trying to rush through the story mode. * Why the fuck am I getting quest notifications about DLC content while I'm in the tutorial level? * These character models look fugly. Even a famous fantasy RPG on a previous generation console released back in the early 2000s had better looking character models with more realistic looking faces than this game. * The Arena is by far the most fun sidequest in the game.
